title: Proof pages for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: What a B2B SaaS proof page must show
excerpt: A proof page needs a constraint, a decision, and the product in use. Screenshots without a decision are decoration. End on how a similar buyer books a demo.
primaryKeyword: B2B SaaS company case study page
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall. The article is about tying a proof page to one decision, not a loose gallery.
caption: A proof page connects a constraint to a choice the way a string connects screens. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a B2B case study include?
faqs.answer: Open with the constraint that was already there, then the decision you made, including an option you refused. Show the product screen that embodies that decision. Close by telling a similar buyer how to book a demo and when the decision would not transfer.

faqs.question: Are screenshots enough for a proof page?
faqs.answer: A gallery of screens shows that a product exists. It does not show judgment. If a frame has no caption stating the decision, move it to a tour or a release note and keep the proof page on one fork.

faqs.question: Can you publish a case study without metrics?
faqs.answer: Yes. Describe the change in the workflow and stop. Invented percentages and quotes the customer did not say are worse than a short page with neither. Omit sensitive details rather than replacing them with larger claims.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company case study page should show a constraint, a decision, and the product in use. An operator who already runs software is not moved by a gallery. They want to see what was hard, what you chose, and the screen that resulted. Then they want to know how a buyer in a similar spot can book a demo.

Screenshots without a decision are decoration. A row of interfaces can prove that someone designed a product. It cannot prove that anyone judged a tradeoff. Judgment is what this buyer is shopping for, because they are about to make a tradeoff of their own.

## Three parts, in this order

Open with the constraint. Follow with the decision. Close the story on the product doing the job, and point a similar buyer to the demo. That order respects the way an operator reads. They grant attention when the problem sounds like theirs. They withdraw it when the page opens with a compliment.

Keep one story per page. A roundup of logos can exist somewhere else. This page is one situation, told far enough that a stranger could retell the constraint and the choice. If you cannot retell it in a minute, you do not have a case yet. You have notes.

Nielsen Norman Group's research summary on how long people stay is a good editor. Visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds unless the page shows its value immediately. On a proof page, the value is the constraint in the first screen. The logo, the year, and a vague outcome line do not hold anyone who has software of their own to get back to.

Name the kind of team and the kind of job. A finance team closing the month. A support lead triaging a shared inbox. You can change identifying details when a customer requires it. You should not change the constraint into something generic. "A fast-growing company wanted to scale" is not a constraint. "The approval sat in email, so the record and the decision drifted apart" is.

## The constraint

Write the constraint as a limit that was already there before you arrived. The tool they had. The rule they could not break. The hour the work consumed. The audit that failed. The fact that two teams kept two versions of the same record.

Be specific about the cost in their week. Extra exports. A meeting that only existed to reconcile. A queue nobody owned. Operators recognize costs. They do not recognize "pain points" as a phrase, because the phrase has been emptied.

Say what they had already tried, if you know it. A spreadsheet. A stricter process. A different tool that solved a neighboring job and missed this one. The tried-and-failed step keeps you honest. It stops the story from pretending the buyer was waiting in a blank room.

Leave out drama you cannot source. Leave out numbers you would not publish with their permission. A proof page with invented percentages is worse than a short page with none. If you have a true before-and-after and they agree to it, use it. If you do not, describe the change in the workflow and stop.

The constraint should be one they still see in other buyers. If the story is a snowflake, it will not help the next demo. Pick stories that rhyme with the homepage job. If the homepage shows approvals, the proof page should be about an approval constraint, not about a rebrand that happened the same year.

## The decision

The decision is the part teams skip because it feels less shiny than the final screen. It is the part the operator reads twice. What did you refuse? What did you choose, and what did that choice cost?

Write one real fork. You could have added a custom status for every team, and you refused, because the queue would become unreadable. You put the decision on a single record instead. Or you kept their existing login and refused a separate password. The fork should be visible in the product afterward.

Name who made the call and what they needed to see. The operator on their side. The person on yours. A proof page that says "we partnered to drive alignment" has not named a decision. Replace the sentence with the fork.

Include the option you did not take, in a sentence. The unused option is how a reader tests whether the choice was judgment or habit. If every decision is the feature you already wanted to build, the story is an ad. If one decision was a no, the story starts to sound like work.

Google's people-first guidance favors content that demonstrates first-hand experience. A decision you were in the room for can show that. A polished recap written from a press release cannot. If you were not in the room, interview the person who was, or do not publish the page. Borrowed certainty reads as thin to this buyer, who sits in those rooms themselves.

## The product in use

After the decision, show the screen that embodies it. One screen, cropped to the job. Annotate it in a sentence beside the image, not in a paragraph of callouts that cover the interface. "The approver sees the record, the amount, and the single action. The side statuses we refused are not here."

A second screen can show the consequence. The queue after the decision. The admin view that stayed simple. Two screens are a story. Eight screens are a tour, and tours blur the decision you worked to explain.

Use a real interface. If you must blur a name or a figure, blur the secret and keep the structure. A mock that tidies the product into a poster breaks the proof. The operator is comparing the screen to the software they already trust. A fantasy UI loses that comparison.

Say what did not change. The next-door system. The person's title. The cadence of the meeting. Proof that claims a transformed company from one screen is the kind of proof this buyer has learned to ignore. A changed step is enough.

Place the screen after the words that explain it. A picture first, with the constraint buried below, makes the page a gallery again. The order is the argument. Constraint, decision, screen.

## Why a screenshot gallery fails

A gallery feels generous. It says look at everything we made. The operator cannot tell which screen was the hard one. They also cannot tell whether the screens belong to the same job. Equal frames mean equal importance, and that is rarely true.

Galleries also invite the feature grid back in through a side door. Each shot becomes a tile. The job disappears. You are back to a catalog, which is the thing the homepage was supposed to refuse.

If you have many screens you are proud of, choose. The others can live in a product tour with its own title, clearly marked as a tour. The proof page stays a decision. Mixing the two modes produces a long page that feels informative and persuades no one.

Captions do the sorting. If you cannot write a caption that states the decision the screen carries, the screen does not belong on this page. It might belong in a release note. Those are different documents.

## End on a similar buyer

The last section is not a slogan. It is a handoff. Say who this story resembles. A team with the approval in email. A record that splits across two tools. Invite that reader to book a demo, and say what the demo will reuse from the story. You will look at their constraint. You will say whether the same decision fits, or whether their case is the one you would refuse.

Offer a reason the decision might not transfer. Different compliance rules. A volume the screen was not built for. The willingness to say "not this" is part of the proof. An operator who sees the fence will book a better call, or will correctly decline.

Give them the practical next step in one line. What to bring. A sketch of the current step. No attachment required to book. The proof page has already asked them to read. Do not ask for a proposal before the conversation.

Link the demo the same way everywhere else on the site. The same label. The same promise. A proof page that invents a new verb for the same calendar makes the company feel stitched together from campaigns.

## What you may not invent

Publish only what you can say in front of the customer and in front of the next buyer. No invented metrics. No quotes you wrote for them. No timeline that flatters the project. If a detail is sensitive, omit it. Do not replace it with a fuzzier claim that sounds larger.

If you have no permission to name the company, say the kind of team and keep the constraint. Unnamed can still be specific. Fictional cannot. A composite that blends three customers into a hero is a story, and it should not wear the costume of a case.

Keep the page short enough to reread. A proof page that passes two thousand words has usually added a second topic. Split it. One constraint. One decision. One product in use. Then the demo.

Once a proof page exists, it only works if a buyer can find it without a tour of the sitemap. The labels in the header decide that. Read [how navigation should map the jobs this buyer already has](/blog/navigation-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you bury the story under a menu called resources.

To see the same standard applied to public project pages, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). A visitor should be able to find the constraint and the choice, not only the final frame.
